## Purpose {.unnumbered .unlisted}

_Why can a safety check miss its deadline even when it runs on its own processor core?_

A correct refusal computed too late does not stop the motion it was meant to prevent. Separating a learned proposer from its permission path in software does not make the two independent while they still share memory, electrical power, clocks, or cooling. A burst of inference can then delay the check that should stop the machine, heat from the accelerator can slow the core that runs that check for seconds after the burst has ended, and a single supply or reset fault can silence both paths at once. None of these couplings appears on a software architecture diagram, and none shows up in average utilization, so a safety argument that has never been loaded on its real silicon rests on an untested premise. Moving the check to separate hardware removes some couplings and adds others, a communication delay and a longer chain of supplies and wiring, so no placement is independent by construction. Where each workload runs therefore decides whether the permission path can still refuse in time, and an action that crosses the causal boundary on a late refusal cannot be taken back.

{{< pagebreak >}}

::: {.callout-learning-objectives}

- Explain why average bus utilization cannot bound a deadline, and identify which contention mechanism (bandwidth queueing, bank conflicts, or shared-cache miss handling) threatens a declared worst-case execution time
- Evaluate whether shared power and reset paths can defeat a selected permission placement
- Analyze thermal coupling and clock throttling hysteresis between multi-tenant workloads across disparate physical timescales
- Size a windowed watchdog's service window from measured completion jitter for a non-blocking lock-free record exchange
- Select among static reservation, spatial partitioning, workload reduction, and physical silicon relocation from measured interference and timing allowances, and allocate the selected placement's dispatch-to-admission interval against the stopping budget
- Design an adversarial stress campaign whose falsification threshold is the permission path's declared worst-case execution time ($C_{\text{wcet}}$)
- Construct a placement record formalizing the deployment envelope that scopes loaded observed maxima, thermal headroom, bus arbitration, mitigations, and untested conditions for release review

## The Silicon Substrate {#sec-placement-silicon-substrate}

Workload placement decides which silicon executes each computation on a machine, and with that choice, which memories, clocks, supplies, and heat paths each computation shares with the others. In most computing systems placement is a performance question. In a physical AI system it is also a safety question, because the guarantees of @sec-enforcement (the barrier filter, the stopping reservation, and the fallback ladder) hold only while the permission path finishes its check inside its deadline on every tick. A check that finishes late leaves the drives executing the last admitted command while the machine covers distance its stopping budget never reserved.

The hardware trend runs against that condition. A heterogeneous system-on-chip (SoC) integrates application processors, neural accelerators, real-time cores, and in some products an isolated safety island on one die, where they share memory controllers, caches, supply rails, clock governors, and the package that carries away their heat. Integration lowers cost, board area, and communication delay, and it reconnects, through shared hardware, the two paths that the software architecture keeps apart. The central question of placement is whether the permission path can keep its deadline and its authority to refuse while the proposer runs at full load on hardware the two paths share. A block diagram cannot answer it. The answer is a bound on interference, which analysis can support and a loaded test can refute, and the chapter builds it in stages: an inventory of what each candidate placement leaves shared, the mechanisms by which memory, power, and heat couple the paths on timescales from nanoseconds to hours, the contract by which separated paths exchange records, the remedies and their prices, the test that could falsify the claim, and the record that carries the result to release review.

On the warehouse mobile manipulator, the software architecture diagram draws the proposal boundary between the Brain and the Nervous System as a clean dashed line, and the design already runs the permission path on a discrete safety microcontroller beside the application SoC. Both of the machine's jobs show what that choice guards against. For the Class 1 base, a memory crossbar stall during feature extraction would delay the permission path's refusal while the loaded base closes on a rack end, and every tick of delay beyond the one the stopping budget counts is distance it never reserved. For the Class 2 arm, an accelerator burst that evicted the permission path's tables from a shared cache would delay the contact check while the gripper presses on the spring-latched cage door. The shared die is the alternative the machine must be able to reject on evidence, and the discrete controller is a claim it must support rather than assume.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ Hardware execution cadences and microcontroller timing loops were defined in @sec-nervous-cadences.
:::

A separate core is not a separate failure domain. It may still wait for memory, slow with a shared clock, or lose power when another core becomes busy. Software access permissions determine who may read an address; the interconnect and memory controller determine when the read proceeds. Memory protection and operating system process isolation give each path a private address space, which is spatial partitioning; they do not give it private time on the hardware it shares, which is temporal partitioning, and a safety argument needs both [@kopetz2011real]. Neither establishes operational independence by itself. On a heterogeneous die,[^fn-place-system-chip] **operational independence**\index{Operational independence!definition} requires that proposal-side activity cannot push enforcement execution beyond its hard physical deadline, and that proposal-side crashes or thermal overruns cannot disable the permission path's authority to refuse.

[^fn-place-system-chip]: **Heterogeneous System-on-Chip Architecture**\index{Heterogeneous system-on-chip!architecture}\index{System-on-Chip (SoC)!heterogeneous compute}: Heterogeneous SoCs integrate multiple distinct compute domains onto a single silicon substrate, combining high-throughput application processors and neural accelerators with deterministic real-time safety islands. Although memory management units isolate software address spaces across domains, hardware subcomponents continue to share power distribution networks, clock distribution trees, and DRAM controllers. Under peak cognitive burst workloads, uncoordinated resource contention across these shared physical structures can degrade real-time response times beyond critical physical deadlines.

A placement claim must therefore name the resources that could delay or disable enforcement and the conditions that bound their interference. The shared die and the machine's discrete controller are competing hypotheses about those dependencies, not interchangeable processor choices, and testing either one starts from what each path must compute and how much time it has to do it.

## Proposal and Permission Co-location on Shared Silicon {#sec-placement-two-paths-one-die}

The mobile manipulator must keep checking clearance while its proposal model computes the next chunk. The architectural overview established why these jobs need separate authority; placement asks whether the hardware can preserve that separation in time. Each path's work and timing allowance determine how much interference its placement can tolerate.

```{python}
#| label: calc-placement-machine-paths
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ MACHINE PATHS: PROPOSAL AND PERMISSION BUDGETS
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-placement-two-paths-one-die, @sec-placement-isolation-decisions,
# │          @sec-placement-hardware-allocation, @sec-placement-fallacies-pitfalls,
# │          @sec-placement-summary
# │
# │ Goal: Size the running machine's two paths from the registry before any
# │       contention: the chunk policy on the application processor and the
# │       enforcer tick on the discrete safety MCU.
# │ Show: 135 µs unloaded = 40 + 80 + 15 µs = 54,000 cycles at 400 MHz, against
# │       a declared 250 µs WCET and a chosen 400 µs deadline in the 1 ms tick.
# │       The permission path's isolated rail holds up for 2 s (a selected
# │       premise recorded here; decided in Ch2, sized in Ch12). The 5 ms
# │       renewal-jitter allowance tolerates at most a 12.5 percent stretch of
# │       the 40 ms chunk inference (Ch8's HostContentionAllowance).
# │ How: Registry fields of the warehouse mobile manipulator and its aisle
# │      scenario; the three enforcer sub-costs are chapter-local.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import microsecond, millisecond, second, hertz
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt_int, fmt_latency, fmt_frequency, fmt_percent, check

RM = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator
AISLE = Embodied.Scenario.WarehouseAisle

class PlacementMachine:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    chunk_rate = RM.chunk_rate  # category: chosen
    chunk_inference = RM.chunk_inference_latency  # category: illustrative (P99, vision included)
    chunk_horizon = RM.chunk_horizon  # category: chosen
    permission_rate = RM.permission_rate  # category: chosen
    mcu_clock = RM.permission_mcu.compute.clock_rate  # category: illustrative (reference class)
    tick = AISLE.t_tick  # category: chosen
    t_bus = AISLE.t_bus  # category: illustrative
    lease = AISLE.t_lease  # category: chosen
    unloaded = AISLE.enforcer_unloaded  # category: illustrative
    wcet = AISLE.enforcer_wcet  # category: chosen (declared, not measured)
    deadline = AISLE.enforcer_deadline  # category: chosen
    self_watchdog = AISLE.mcu_self_watchdog  # category: chosen
    rail_holdup = RM.permission_rail_holdup  # category: chosen (permission-rail hold-up)
    renewal_jitter = 5 * millisecond  # category: chosen (renewal-jitter allowance of the lease rule, @sec-nervous-coupled-budget)
    sense = 40 * microsecond  # scenario assumption; category: illustrative (encoders, IMU, evidence epoch)
    constraint = 80 * microsecond  # scenario assumption; category: illustrative
    write = 15 * microsecond  # scenario assumption; category: illustrative (drive-frame staging)

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    chunk_period = (1 / chunk_rate).to(millisecond)
    chunk_slack = (chunk_period - chunk_inference).to(millisecond)
    unloaded_sum = (sense + constraint + write).to(microsecond)
    unloaded_slack = (deadline - unloaded).to(microsecond)
    wcet_margin = (deadline - wcet).to(microsecond)
    unloaded_cycles = (unloaded * mcu_clock).to("dimensionless").magnitude
    min_chunk_rate = (1 / lease).to(hertz)
    compute_after_sense = (constraint + write).to(microsecond)
    contention_stretch = (renewal_jitter / chunk_inference).to("dimensionless").magnitude

    # ┌── 3. GUARD ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    check(
        abs((unloaded_sum - unloaded).to(microsecond).magnitude) < 1e-9, "Sense + constraint + write must equal the registry's 135 µs unloaded cycle."
    )
    check(abs(unloaded.to(microsecond).magnitude - 135.0) < 1e-9, "Canon: 135 µs unloaded.")
    check(abs(unloaded_cycles - 54_000) < 1e-6, "Canon: 135 µs = 54,000 cycles at 400 MHz.")
    check(wcet < deadline < tick, "Declared WCET inside the deadline, deadline inside the tick.")
    check(
        abs(wcet.to(microsecond).magnitude - 250.0) < 1e-9 and abs(deadline.to(microsecond).magnitude - 400.0) < 1e-9,
        "Canon: 250 µs WCET, 400 µs deadline.",
    )
    check(abs(chunk_slack.to(millisecond).magnitude - 10.0) < 1e-9, "The 40 ms chunk inference leaves 10 ms of the 50 ms period.")
    check(
        chunk_period < lease, "Lease rule: the lease outlasts one chunk period, leaving the renewal-jitter allowance that absorbs the proposal link."
    )
    check(abs(rail_holdup.to(second).magnitude - 2.0) < 1e-9, "Canon (D15): the permission rail holds up for 2.0 s.")
    check(chunk_period + renewal_jitter < lease, "Lease rule: chunk period plus the 5 ms renewal-jitter allowance fits inside the lease.")
    check(
        abs(contention_stretch - 0.125) < 1e-9,
        "Matches Ch8 HostContentionAllowance: 5 ms of jitter is a 12.5 percent stretch of the 40 ms inference.",
    )

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    chunk_rate_str = fmt_frequency(chunk_rate, precision=0)
    chunk_period_str = fmt_latency(chunk_period, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    chunk_inference_str = fmt_latency(chunk_inference, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    chunk_slack_str = fmt_latency(chunk_slack, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    chunk_horizon_str = fmt_int(chunk_horizon)
    permission_rate_str = fmt_frequency(permission_rate, precision=0)
    mcu_clock_str = fmt_frequency(mcu_clock, precision=0)
    tick_str = fmt_latency(tick, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    t_bus_str = fmt_latency(t_bus, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    lease_str = fmt_latency(lease, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    min_chunk_rate_str = fmt_frequency(min_chunk_rate, precision=1)
    sense_str = fmt_latency(sense, unit=microsecond, precision=0)
    constraint_str = fmt_latency(constraint, unit=microsecond, precision=0)
    write_str = fmt_latency(write, unit=microsecond, precision=0)
    compute_after_sense_str = fmt_latency(compute_after_sense, unit=microsecond, precision=0)
    unloaded_str = fmt_latency(unloaded, unit=microsecond, precision=0)
    unloaded_cycles_str = fmt_int(unloaded_cycles)
    unloaded_slack_str = fmt_latency(unloaded_slack, unit=microsecond, precision=0)
    wcet_str = fmt_latency(wcet, unit=microsecond, precision=0)
    wcet_margin_str = fmt_latency(wcet_margin, unit=microsecond, precision=0)
    deadline_str = fmt_latency(deadline, unit=microsecond, precision=0)
    self_watchdog_str = fmt_latency(self_watchdog, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    rail_holdup_str = fmt_latency(rail_holdup, unit=second, precision=0)
    renewal_jitter_str = fmt_latency(renewal_jitter, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    contention_stretch_pct_str = fmt_percent(contention_stretch, precision=1)
```

### Proposal and permission execution profiles

The mobile manipulator partitions its control across two paths with conflicting requirements. The proposal path runs the chunk policy on the application processor at `{python} PlacementMachine.chunk_rate_str`, taking the navigation and wrist camera streams and emitting base velocity and arm joint targets together. Its P99 inference, vision included, takes `{python} PlacementMachine.chunk_inference_str` (illustrative; see the Reader Guide) of each `{python} PlacementMachine.chunk_period_str` chunk period; it holds no direct hardware authority over the drives and runs in unprivileged user space. The permission path runs on the discrete safety microcontroller (MCU) at `{python} PlacementMachine.permission_rate_str`. Each tick it checks the admitted trajectory and any eligible replacement against the stopping envelope of @sec-enforcement-stopping-envelopes and stages the admitted setpoints for the EtherCAT frame to the drives. It must finish inside a chosen `{python} PlacementMachine.deadline_str` deadline within its `{python} PlacementMachine.tick_str` tick, and it runs in a privileged real-time execution domain on a dual-core lockstep controller,[^fn-place-asild-lockstep] whose comparator diagnostics cover selected divergent execution faults, because an envelope check cannot detect a fault in the core that executes it. Only the permission path holds memory-mapped input-output (MMIO)\index{Memory-mapped I/O} access to the fieldbus master that carries drive commands.

::: {#dfn-placement-heterogeneous-silicon-partitioning .callout-definition title="Heterogeneous silicon partitioning"}

***Heterogeneous silicon partitioning***\index{Heterogeneous silicon partitioning!definition}\index{Silicon partitioning!definition} is the architectural allocation of stochastic, high-capacity cognitive workloads (perception, learned policy evaluation) and deterministic safety loops (safety invariant checks, admission and fallback) across specialized execution domains isolated in hardware.

1.  **Significance**: Placing high-capacity neural deliberation and real-time safety enforcement on the same general-purpose operating system or compute engine creates common-mode failures. Kernel thread preemption, dynamic memory allocation, and time-slicing between accelerator contexts add tail delay that no measured average bounds, and a permission path exposed to that tail can miss its physical control deadline.
2.  **Distinction**: Unlike logical software process isolation (such as Linux containers or POSIX process priorities), silicon partitioning enforces isolation across independent hardware registers, tightly-coupled static memories (TCM), and dedicated peripheral buses.
3.  **Common pitfall**: Assuming multi-core CPU affinity provides true failure-domain separation, when the cores still share caches, memory controllers, clock trees, and power rails.

:::

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ The sub-millisecond execution deadline of the CBF-QP enforcer was established in @sec-enforcement-minimal-intervention.
:::

The two processors run the stacks introduced in @sec-nervous-silicon-partitioning. Proposal inference, scene-map updates, telemetry, and networking run on the application processor under Linux. A real-time kernel can reduce scheduler latency, but it does not bound every driver, memory, or shared-hardware delay.[^fn-place-preempt-rt] Zero-copy buffers reduce copying traffic without eliminating competition for the underlying memory controller.

Enforcement and sensor validation run on the discrete safety microcontroller as bare-metal firmware behind a hardware memory protection unit,[^fn-place-memory-partitioning] with encoder interfaces, the IMU, and hardware timer channels wired to its dedicated peripheral pins. Each proposal reaches the microcontroller over a board-level link and is published through the seqlock mailbox of @sec-nervous-cadences. No dynamic random-access memory (DRAM)\index{DRAM}\index{Dynamic random-access memory|see{DRAM}} is shared between the paths. The protection unit constrains access to local state; the separate bus removes the host's memory traffic from the enforcer's execution path.

Whole-plan admission is a separate workload from the permission tick. The illustrative whole-plan validation interval in @sec-planning-horizon-tradeoff cannot execute as an unbroken task inside the millisecond loop. Its scheduler must preserve the tick through bounded, interruptible work or an independently assessed admission domain, followed by a final current-state and evidence check before activation. The allocation ledger must include the trajectory buffer, resident fallback, admission workspace, and worst-case interruption costs. The producer period does not establish the interval between successful admissions. Qualification must show that transfer, admission, and activation preserve the renewal bound; the chosen tick deadline alone cannot establish it.

The full scene map remains on the application processor. The permission path receives only a bounded local evidence snapshot whose coverage, uncertainty, observation epoch, expiry, and integrity have been checked for the proposed motion and its fallback. The host map update, snapshot conversion, transport, admission, local storage, and per-tick query costs require separate ledger entries. A host query cannot enter the tick as an unbounded dependency. The MCU must reject motion outside the snapshot's supported region or validity, and its memory inventory must show that the local snapshot and resident trajectories fit alongside the enforcement code.

The supply design places the microcontroller, drive logic, and spring-brake coils on the isolated rail of @sec-body-archetype-matrix, with a selected local hold-up of `{python} PlacementMachine.rail_holdup_str` and no proposal-side load. Qualification must show that motor and accelerator transients on the common battery do not reset this path. That store supports logic and brake release during the selected stop; it does not supply traction power. The powered deceleration of @sec-enforcement-fallback-ladder additionally requires a surviving drive-energy path and a qualified destination for regenerative energy. Loss of either premise invokes a separately qualified fault response, not the normal stopping-distance claim.

On the unloaded machine the computational budgets appear generous. Illustrative sub-costs on the safety microcontroller put reading the encoders, the IMU, and the proposal's evidence epoch at `{python} PlacementMachine.sense_str`, evaluating the constraints at `{python} PlacementMachine.constraint_str`, and staging the admitted setpoints for the drive frame at `{python} PlacementMachine.write_str`. The enforcer's unloaded cycle totals `{python} PlacementMachine.unloaded_str`, which at the microcontroller's `{python} PlacementMachine.mcu_clock_str` clock is `{python} PlacementMachine.unloaded_cycles_str` cycles. Against the `{python} PlacementMachine.deadline_str` deadline, the unloaded path leaves `{python} PlacementMachine.unloaded_slack_str` of slack, and the declared worst-case execution time of `{python} PlacementMachine.wcet_str`, the selected budget of @sec-enforcement-minimal-intervention, still leaves `{python} PlacementMachine.wcet_margin_str`. On the application processor, the chunk policy's `{python} PlacementMachine.chunk_inference_str` inference leaves `{python} PlacementMachine.chunk_slack_str` of its `{python} PlacementMachine.chunk_period_str` period. These sub-costs form the simplified interference example below, not an integrated execution measurement. The local spatial-query allocation of @sec-memory must also fit the cyclic budget. Qualification must measure the complete cycle, identifying which query costs are included in constraint evaluation and adding any that are separate; neither the unloaded sum nor the query allocation alone establishes the declared bound.

### Shared microarchitectural failure domains and cyber-physical attack surfaces

Assigning tasks to separate processor cores does not create independent failure domains if the silicon infrastructure is shared.[^fn-std-cast-32a] @sec-nervous-hardware-isolation traced these common-cause paths on the machine's board, where separate packages and the isolated rail cut the memory and supply paths. On a shared die, the rejected option for this machine, they move inside one package. The real-time core executes instructions independently from the application processor, yet both cores rely on common hardware services:

- *Interrupt and memory service:* Camera, accelerator, and logging traffic can delay dispatch or memory reads unless arbitration bounds their interference.
- *Clock and thermal control:* A shared governor can slow the permission core when another domain heats the package.
- *Supply and reset:* Current steps or a host-triggered reset can disable both paths unless the electrical and reset domains remain independent.

These same dependencies create a **cyber-physical attack vector**\index{Cyber-physical security!shared-die attack surface}\index{Hardware security!side channels and DoS}. A compromised proposal process can deliberately generate the memory traffic or accelerator switching that an ordinary workload produces accidentally. Memory saturation delays enforcement, while a current step can induce $L \cdot dI/dt$ droop on a shared rail. The isolation claim must therefore cover adversarial demand within the proposal domain's permitted resource access; trusting its normal workload does not establish a hardware bound.

Functional-safety engineering has names for this inventory and for the split it protects. On this machine the rated part is deliberately narrow. The admission checks that project and test each learned proposal carry no integrity claim of their own; the certified stop functions of the drives and the safety scanner carry the formal protective claim. The one rated function on the microcontroller is its lease-expiry and heartbeat-loss watchdog, which commands a safe torque off or a controlled stop on the drives when renewal stops. Keeping that rated function apart from everything that carries no integrity claim, the learned proposer and the admission checks included, is a decomposition of the safety requirement, and a decomposition is valid only if the elements are sufficiently independent. Placement decides whether they are. The search for resources whose single fault or overload could defeat both elements at once is a **dependent failure analysis**\index{Dependent failure analysis!placement}\index{Common-cause failure!shared silicon}, which ISO 26262 Part 9 requires for exactly this purpose [@iso26262]; IEC 61508 treats the same concern as common-cause failure between redundant channels [@iec61508]. The inventory in this chapter is that analysis, carried out on the machine's hardware and priced in its timing budget.

[^fn-std-cast-32a]: **Avionic Multicore Certification**\index{Multicore interference!FAA AC 20-193 / CAST-32A}\index{Worst-case execution time!multicore certification}: FAA Advisory Circular AC 20-193, issued in 2024 to replace the earlier CAST-32A position paper and aligned with EASA's AMC 20-193, formalizes multicore interference analysis for safety-critical avionics [@faa2024ac20193]. The guidance requires bounding worst-case execution times by demonstrating that shared caches, interconnect crossbars, and memory controllers cannot cause critical tasks to overrun execution deadlines. Without hardware-enforced quality-of-service partitions or dedicated interconnect channels, cross-core memory traffic invalidates a single-core timing bound.

[^fn-place-preempt-rt]: **PREEMPT_RT**\index{Preempt RT!kernel latency}: A Linux real-time configuration reduces some scheduler latencies, but its tail depends on kernel, drivers, workload, and shared hardware. No portable sub-$50\,\mu\text{s}$ or bare-metal comparison follows without measurement.

[^fn-place-memory-partitioning]: **Hardware memory protection and IOMMU domains**\index{Memory Protection Unit!spatial isolation}\index{IOMMU!DMA isolation}: Physical silicon structures that enforce spatial address isolation. While an on-chip Memory Protection Unit (MPU) confines CPU thread execution to bounded memory segments, an Input-Output Memory Management Unit (IOMMU) translates and polices direct memory access (DMA) requests from peripheral bus masters (such as PCIe neural accelerators or camera deserializers), physically preventing an untrusted device from corrupting safety state buffers.

[^fn-place-asild-lockstep]: **Dual-core lockstep**\index{Lockstep processor!fault detection}: Two cores can execute matching instruction streams while comparator logic detects selected divergences. Detection coverage, delay, shared-rail vulnerability, and diagnostic response depend on the device and the application safety case, so lockstep is one element of the argument for the microcontroller's rated watchdog and stop trigger, not the whole of it.

### Four candidate placements against one shared-resource inventory

Because software process isolation cannot remove these hardware couplings, the placement of the permission path becomes the primary architectural defense. Four candidates are worth comparing for the machine's permission loop, and @tbl-13-placement-candidates runs each against the same inventory.

(a) *Shared application cores* expose the permission loop to the kernel and driver scheduling tail described earlier, a tail that can push it past not only the `{python} PlacementMachine.deadline_str` deadline but the `{python} PlacementMachine.tick_str` tick itself.

(b) *A real-time cluster in the host clock and power domain* keeps its own cores but shares the die's cache hierarchy, memory controller, core rail, clock governor, and thermal path. @Sec-placement-resource-contention prices its memory exposure, and @sec-placement-thermal-timing-coupling shows the clock throttle that rejects it.

(c) *An on-die safety island* is the design current automotive and industrial SoCs actually offer, and it is a much stronger candidate than (b). The Functional Safety Island of NVIDIA's Orin-class SoCs, for example, groups four dual-core lockstep Cortex-R52 processors, each with its own tightly coupled memory, around 3 MB of on-island SRAM, and runs them from a dedicated crystal and a dedicated voltage rail, with firewalls that block access from the rest of the die [@nvidia2023drivefsi]. The application governor cannot throttle that clock, and a tick whose code and data stay in island memory never waits on the host's DRAM. What still couples the island to the proposer is shorter but not empty: the die temperature and package it shares, the reset and boot chain that brings it up, the on-chip fabric and firewall through which proposals and any island DMA to external memory pass, and the board supply behind its rail. Admitting the island would take evidence on each of those rows: the configured firewall and memory map read back from registers, reset and power sequencing traced to their controlling hardware, and the loaded stress campaign of @sec-placement-testing-separation run with the island ticking.

(d) *A discrete safety microcontroller* removes every on-die row and pays in transport, a board-level link from the application processor that none of the on-die options needs and that @sec-placement-isolation-decisions budgets.

@Fig-13-placement-resource-map places the four candidates on one board, so that each row of the inventory below has a physical location. Everything tinted as a consequence sits on the die or behind its memory controller, where a tick on candidate (a) or (b) can lose it; the safety island escapes most of those rows but still shares the fabric and the package; the discrete controller shares only the battery.

```{python}
#| label: calc-placement-resource-map-figure
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ VALUES DRAWN IN THE PLACEMENT RESOURCE MAP (FIGURE GUARD)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @fig-13-placement-resource-map
# │
# │ Goal: Keep the hand-drawn labels of fig13_placement_resource_map.svg
# │       pinned to the registry.
# │ Show: MCU clock 400 MHz, permission tick 1 kHz, permission-rail hold-up 2 s.
# │ How: PlacementMachine fields; a failed check means the SVG label is stale.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim.core.units import second, hertz, ureg
from mlsysim.fmt import check

class PlacementResourceMapFigure:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    PM = PlacementMachine  # category: derived; calc-placement-machine-paths

    # ┌── 3. GUARD ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    check(abs(PM.mcu_clock.to(ureg.megahertz).magnitude - 400.0) < 1e-9, "figure MCU clock label (400 MHz) is stale")
    check(abs(PM.permission_rate.to(hertz).magnitude - 1000.0) < 1e-9, "figure tick-rate label (1 kHz) is stale")
    check(abs(PM.rail_holdup.to(second).magnitude - 2.0) < 1e-9, "figure isolated-rail hold-up label (2 s) is stale")
```

::: {#fig-13-placement-resource-map fig-env="figure" fig-pos="t" fig-cap="**Where each candidate placement runs**: Badges (a) to (d) mark where the permission tick would execute. Tinted blocks are shared with the proposer on the application die (cache, memory controller and external DRAM, clock governor, core rail, reset chain, fabric, and the package's heat path), so a tick placed on the die can lose them to proposal-side load. The safety island carries its own crystal, rail, and memory but remains behind the shared fabric and in the shared package; the discrete controller, the machine's choice, reaches the die only through a checked board link and shares only the battery with it." fig-alt="Block diagram of the machine's compute board. Below them, red-tinted shared blocks: last-level cache, DRAM controller, clock governor, core supply rail, reset and boot chain, on-chip fabric, and die temperature and package, with external LPDDR5 DRAM below the die. Badges a, b, and c mark the application cores, the real-time cluster, and the island. On the right, a separate green discrete safety MCU package, badge d, with lockstep cores at 400 MHz and a 1 kHz tick, TCM, its own clock, a reset supervisor, and a local mailbox, receives a board link from the fabric, drives EtherCAT to the drives, and is fed by an isolated rail with 2 s hold-up. A battery and common board supply bar along the bottom feeds both sides."}
![](images/svg/fig13_placement_resource_map.svg){width="100%"}
:::

: **Dependent-failure inventory of four placements**: Each row is a resource whose fault or overload could delay or disable both the proposer and the permission path. "Separated" means the placement removes the resource from the permission tick's path; it is still a claim that register readback and loaded tests must support. Only the discrete controller removes the die-level rows, and none of the four removes the common board supply. {#tbl-13-placement-candidates tbl-colwidths="[24,14,18,24,20]"}

On technical merit, candidate (c) would serve this machine: it removes every row that the rejected examples of this chapter exploit. The machine uses (d) for a reason that has nothing to do with silicon capability. The safety island is present on the die, but the commercial edge modules that carry the machine's application processor do not enable it for users, and the vendor reserves it for a separate industrial platform (@tbl-13-island-exposure). A safety island the integrator cannot program is not a placement option, so the permission path moves off the module.

| Platform (vendor statement date)  | Safety island on the SoC                          | Available to the integrator | Source              |
|:----------------------------------|:--------------------------------------------------|:----------------------------|:--------------------|
| **Jetson AGX Orin module (2023)** | Cortex-R52 island present                         | No                          | @nvidia2023orinfsi  |
| **IGX Orin platform (2023)**      | Same island                                       | Announced as offered        | @nvidia2023orinfsi  |
| **DRIVE AGX Orin (2023)**         | Island with dedicated crystal and rail, 3 MB SRAM | Yes, through DRIVE OS       | @nvidia2023drivefsi |
| **Jetson Thor module (2026)**     | Not supported                                     | No                          | @nvidia2026thorfsi  |
| **IGX Thor platform (2026)**      | Supported                                         | Yes                         | @nvidia2026thorfsi  |

: **Safety-island exposure on edge AI platforms, as of 2026**: The same silicon can carry an island that one product line exposes and another does not. Which island a placement can use is a property of the module and its software support, not of the SoC's block diagram, and a later edition should refresh this table. {#tbl-13-island-exposure tbl-colwidths="[30,28,20,22]"}

The durable lesson is that platform exposure is itself a placement constraint. A block diagram that shows an isolated domain establishes what the silicon could do, and only the module's documentation and the integrator's access establish what the design can use. The dated fact will change; the obligation to check it before choosing a placement will not.

Principle \ref{pri-vol4-proposal-permission} requires a permission path that learned workloads cannot delay, and the four placements differ precisely in which resources the two paths still share. Even the discrete microcontroller's separation is a claim about timing under load, which only a measurement of its tick under that load can support. Every resource the two paths share has claimants on that tick, and on the on-die candidates the memory system is where they collide first.

## Contention for Shared Resources {#sec-placement-resource-contention}

Had the mobile manipulator placed its permission path on the application SoC, camera DMA, neural weight fetches, telemetry writes, cache writebacks, and enforcement reads would compete for memory service. Their simultaneous bursts determine the queue seen by the enforcer. On the selected machine, those host-side bursts delay the observation and chunk rather than the permission tick. The permission path encounters their effects as evidence age (@sec-perception-cost-ingestion), refusing stale evidence and entering fallback if no admitted chunk renews the lease.

### DRAM bank conflicts, AXI4 burst slicing, and arbiter starvation

```{python}
#| label: calc-placement-dram-timing
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ LPDDR5 ROW-CONFLICT PENALTY ON THE APPLICATION SOC
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-placement-resource-contention, @sec-placement-testing-separation
# │
# │ Goal: Source the row-conflict penalty (t_RP + t_RCD) that the loaded-read
# │       notebook and the stress suite charge, instead of a hand-typed DDR4-era
# │       14 ns.
# │ Show: at LPDDR5-6400 the command clock is 800 MHz (1.25 ns); t_RCD and the
# │       per-bank t_RP are 15 cycles each, 18.75 ns, so a conflict costs
# │       37.5 ns. 256 bits x 6400 MT/s = 204.8 GB/s, matching the registry's
# │       rounded 204 GB/s.
# │ How: Hardware.Tech.Memory.LPDDR5_6400 (JESD209-5 timings as encoded in
# │      the Ramulator 2.0 preset: nRCD = 15, nRPpb = 15, tCK = 1250 ps); bus
# │      width and per-pin data rate from the brain SoC's registry memory
# │      (Jetson AGX Orin technical brief: 256-bit LPDDR5, 204.8 GB/s).
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
import math
from mlsysim.core.units import Q_, nanosecond
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt, fmt_int, check

RM = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator

class PlacementDramTiming:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    lpddr5 = Hardware.Tech.Memory.LPDDR5_6400  # category: datasheet (JESD209-5 via Ramulator 2.0 preset)
    pin_rate = RM.brain_soc.memory.pin_data_rate  # category: datasheet (registry; Orin technical brief)
    bus_width = RM.brain_soc.memory.bus_width  # category: datasheet (registry; Orin technical brief)
    bandwidth = RM.brain_soc.memory.bandwidth  # category: datasheet (registry, rounded)

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    t_ck = lpddr5.t_ck.to(nanosecond)
    t_rcd = lpddr5.t_rcd.to(nanosecond)
    t_rp = lpddr5.t_rp.to(nanosecond)
    n_rcd = (t_rcd / t_ck).to("dimensionless").magnitude
    n_rp_pb = (t_rp / t_ck).to("dimensionless").magnitude
    t_conflict = (t_rp + t_rcd).to(nanosecond)
    t_min = lpddr5.t_rcd_min.to(nanosecond)  # category: datasheet (JESD209-5 analog minimum, t_RCD = t_RPpb)
    n_min_cycles = math.ceil((t_min / t_ck).to("dimensionless").magnitude)
    data_rate_mts = pin_rate.to("Mbit/s").magnitude  # one bit per transfer per pin
    bus_bandwidth = (bus_width * pin_rate / Q_("1 bit")).to("GB/s")

    # ┌── 3. GUARD ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    check(abs(n_rcd - 15) < 1e-9 and abs(n_rp_pb - 15) < 1e-9, "t_RCD and t_RP are 15 command-clock cycles each.")
    check(abs(t_conflict.magnitude - 37.5) < 1e-9, "t_RP + t_RCD = 2 x 15 x 1.25 ns = 37.5 ns at LPDDR5-6400.")
    check(
        n_min_cycles == round(n_rcd) and abs(lpddr5.t_rp_min.to(nanosecond).magnitude - t_min.magnitude) < 1e-9,
        "The 18 ns minimum rounds up to the 15-cycle clocked timing, for t_RCD and t_RPpb alike.",
    )
    check(abs(bus_bandwidth.magnitude - 204.8) < 1e-9, "256 bits at 6400 MT/s is 204.8 GB/s.")
    check(abs((bus_bandwidth / bandwidth).to("dimensionless").magnitude - 1) < 0.005, "Bus arithmetic matches the registry's rounded 204 GB/s.")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    t_rp_str = fmt(t_rp.magnitude, precision=2)
    t_min_str = fmt(t_min.magnitude, precision=0)
    t_ck_str = fmt(t_ck.magnitude, precision=2)
    n_rp_str = fmt_int(n_rp_pb)
    t_conflict_str = fmt(t_conflict.magnitude, precision=1)
    data_rate_str = fmt_int(data_rate_mts)
```

A small urgent read can wait behind a large transfer even when the memory bus is mostly idle over a longer interval. The deadline depends on the traffic already ahead of that read and on whether the controller lets it pass. On a shared die, **crossbar bus and DRAM bank contention**\index{Crossbar bus and DRAM bank contention!definition} is queuing delay when memory and DMA transactions share an interconnect and controller, and its bound depends on transaction size, queue policy, and bank timing.[^fn-place-dram-bandwidth]

[^fn-place-dram-bandwidth]: **DRAM bank conflicts**\index{DRAM!bank conflicts}: A different row in the same active bank may require precharge and activation before column service. Actual bank mapping, overlap, and scheduling determine the added delay.

Each claimant's average demand follows from its transfer size and event rate. On a shared multi-channel LPDDR5 interface, camera DMA streams, weight fetches at the policy rate, the enforcer's reads, drive writes, cache writebacks, and logging together occupy a modest fraction of theoretical peak bandwidth on average. An engineer who inspects only that average concludes that most of the memory bus remains free. Memory crossbar arbiters and DRAM schedulers do not schedule average rates. They arbitrate discrete, bursty transactions, and two workloads with identical average throughput interfere with radically different latency profiles if one streams in small, sporadic packets while the other arrives in long, saturating blocks. The weight transfers that set the memory wall of @sec-brain-cognitive-pipeline are the long blocks here, and on a shared controller the proposer's throughput limit becomes the permission path's queue.

How long a safety read waits depends on transaction arbitration and DRAM scheduling. An accelerator moving weights in large $256\,\text{KiB}$ tiles generates discrete memory transactions across the internal system interconnect. The example assumes an arbiter that completes each granted burst before serving a different requester.[^fn-hw-axi-burst] Furthermore, while bus protocols provide Quality of Service (QoS) priority signals (`ARQOS`), commodity memory controllers frequently treat these tags as advisory unless strict hardware priority bypass with bounded preemption latency is explicitly certified in register configurations. Whether an in-flight transfer can delay the urgent read, and whether queued tensor transactions can pass it, depends on the selected interconnect and arbiter. AXI burst limits alone do not establish a service-time or starvation bound.

[^fn-hw-axi-burst]: **AXI4 transaction slicing and burst limits**\index{Hardware!AXI4 burst limits}: AXI4 permits INCR bursts of up to 256 beats and forbids a burst from crossing a 4,096-byte address boundary. An aligned $256\,\text{KiB}$ tile transferred using full-width 128-bit ($16$-byte), 256-beat INCR bursts therefore takes 64 transactions. Smaller beats, shorter bursts, or misalignment change that count. In the selected arbitration example, an urgent read waits for the currently granted burst to finish; that scheduling premise is not a universal AXI guarantee.

Every memory request passes through four stages: the requester issues it, the interconnect arbiter grants it a slot, the memory controller queues it, and the target bank serves it. Each DRAM bank holds one open row in its **row buffer**. An LPDDR5 channel has 16 banks, divided into 4 bank groups at the higher data rates, or 8 larger banks, each formed by merging two, in an alternative mode [@steiner2022lpddr5]. A read to the open row (a *row hit*) needs only a column access. A read to a different row of the same bank (a *row conflict*) must first close the open row with a precharge ($t_{\text{RP}}$) and then open the new one with an activation ($t_{\text{RCD}}$). The memory standard sets a minimum time in nanoseconds for each step, `{python} PlacementDramTiming.t_min_str` ns for both, and the controller can only wait whole cycles of its command clock. At the `{python} PlacementDramTiming.data_rate_str` MT/s data rate of the machine's application SoC, that clock ticks every `{python} PlacementDramTiming.t_ck_str` ns, each step rounds up to `{python} PlacementDramTiming.n_rp_str` cycles, or `{python} PlacementDramTiming.t_rp_str` ns, and a conflict adds `{python} PlacementDramTiming.t_conflict_str` ns [@luo2024ramulator]. Write recovery, bus turnaround, and bank-group spacing add further terms that @sec-appendix-systems-dram develops.

The controller also decides the order of service. Controllers that use **first-ready, first-come-first-served (FR-FCFS)**\index{FR-FCFS scheduling!definition} scheduling serve ready row hits before older requests that need a new row, which maximizes throughput [@rixner2000memory]. A streaming accelerator supplies an unbroken run of row hits across its weight matrices, so an FR-FCFS scheduler can keep passing the safety core's sporadic read until an internal starvation counter expires. Under a FIFO queue that lets no later arrival pass the safety read, the idealized wait is
$$t_{\text{queue}} = \sum_{k \in \mathcal{Q}} \frac{B_k}{\text{BW}_{\text{peak}}} + N_{\text{conflicts}} (t_{\text{RP}} + t_{\text{RCD}})$$ {#eq-placement-dram-queuing}
where $\mathcal{Q}$ holds the transactions ahead of the read, $B_k$ is each one's byte count, $N_{\text{conflicts}}$ counts changes to a different row within an already active bank, and $\text{BW}_{\text{peak}}$ is an optimistic service rate. Arbitration overhead and refresh add to the result. Exceeding the sensing allowance first violates the allocation to that subtask; it does not by itself imply that the whole tick misses its deadline. The worked comparison below keeps the sense allocation, declared execution bound, and physical deadline separate.

```{python}
#| label: calc-placement-loaded-read
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ THE PERMISSION PATH'S LOADED READ ON A SHARED DIE (REJECTED PLACEMENT)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-placement-resource-contention, @sec-placement-fallacies-pitfalls
# │
# │ Goal: Charge a FIFO backlog on shared DRAM to the machine's 40 µs sense
# │       allowance and 400 µs deadline, to show why the bound is a property of
# │       the memory controller rather than of the workload.
# │ Show: one backlog of 88 transactions (360,448 bytes) plus three 37.5 ns row
# │       conflicts waits 1.879 µs at the application SoC's 204 GB/s; a 4 KiB
# │       snapshot then reads in 1.899 µs, inside the 40 µs allowance, which
# │       absorbs 21 such backlogs; the declared 250 µs WCET is crossed after
# │       more than 82 backlogs (155 µs read), refuting the declared bound,
# │       while the deadline holds until more than 162 (305 µs read); priority
# │       bypass cuts the read to 0.04 µs. Confined to one of 16 channels, a
# │       backlog takes 28.4 µs: the allowance absorbs 1, the WCET 5. Bandwidth
# │       queueing alone is a weak threat under interleaving;
# │       @sec-placement-interference-mechanisms prices the strong one.
# │ How: calc_axi_fifo_contention with PlacementMachine's sub-costs; bandwidth is
# │      the brain SoC's registry peak (RM.brain_soc.memory.bandwidth), served
# │      at the full aggregate rate because addresses interleave across all
# │      channels; queue composition and snapshot size are scenario inputs.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
import math
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import Q_, microsecond
from mlsysim.physics.robotics import calc_axi_fifo_contention
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt_int, fmt_latency, check

RM = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator

class PlacementLoadedRead:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    sense = PlacementMachine.sense  # category: illustrative (sense allowance)
    compute_after_sense = PlacementMachine.compute_after_sense  # category: illustrative (80 + 15 µs)
    deadline = PlacementMachine.deadline  # category: chosen
    wcet = PlacementMachine.wcet  # category: chosen (declared WCET, the falsification threshold)
    tile_bytes = 256 * 1024  # category: illustrative (weight tile)
    camera_bytes = 64 * 1024  # category: illustrative
    telemetry_bytes = 32 * 1024  # category: illustrative
    snapshot_bytes = 4 * 1024  # category: illustrative (encoder, IMU, and evidence-epoch snapshot)
    transaction_bytes = 4 * 1024  # category: datasheet (AXI4 4 KiB boundary)
    # Premise: the controller interleaves physical addresses across all its
    # channels, so the backlog and the snapshot are both served at the SoC's
    # aggregate peak rate. A backlog confined to the snapshot's channel would wait
    # longer by the channel count.
    bandwidth = RM.brain_soc.memory.bandwidth  # category: datasheet (application SoC peak DRAM bandwidth)
    bank_switches = 3  # same-bank row conflicts; category: illustrative
    bank_switch_time = PlacementDramTiming.t_conflict  # category: datasheet (LPDDR5-6400 t_RP + t_RCD)
    channel_width = Hardware.Tech.Memory.LPDDR5_6400.channel_width.to("bit").magnitude  # category: datasheet (LPDDR5 x16 channel, registry)
    bus_width_bits = RM.brain_soc.memory.bus_width.to("bit").magnitude  # category: datasheet (registry)

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    result = calc_axi_fifo_contention(
        tile_bytes=tile_bytes,
        camera_bytes=camera_bytes,
        telemetry_bytes=telemetry_bytes,
        safety_read_bytes=snapshot_bytes,
        transaction_bytes=transaction_bytes,
        bandwidth=bandwidth,
        bank_switches=bank_switches,
        bank_switch_time=bank_switch_time,
        compute_time=compute_after_sense,
    )
    backlog_bytes = tile_bytes + camera_bytes + telemetry_bytes
    queue = result["queue_fifo"].to(microsecond)
    own_read = result["own_read"].to(microsecond)
    loaded_read = (queue + own_read).to(microsecond)
    sense_left = (sense - loaded_read).to(microsecond)
    read_ceiling = (deadline - compute_after_sense).to(microsecond)
    wcet_read_ceiling = (wcet - compute_after_sense).to(microsecond)
    backlogs_wcet = math.floor(((wcet_read_ceiling - own_read) / queue).to("dimensionless").magnitude)
    backlogs_sense = math.floor(((sense - own_read) / queue).to("dimensionless").magnitude)
    backlogs_deadline = math.floor(((read_ceiling - own_read) / queue).to("dimensionless").magnitude)
    bypass_read = (result["queue_priority_bypass"] + own_read).to(microsecond)
    # Contrast case: the backlog and the snapshot confined to one channel.
    n_channels = int(round(bus_width_bits / channel_width))
    result_1ch = calc_axi_fifo_contention(
        tile_bytes=tile_bytes,
        camera_bytes=camera_bytes,
        telemetry_bytes=telemetry_bytes,
        safety_read_bytes=snapshot_bytes,
        transaction_bytes=transaction_bytes,
        bandwidth=bandwidth / n_channels,
        bank_switches=bank_switches,
        bank_switch_time=bank_switch_time,
        compute_time=compute_after_sense,
    )
    queue_1ch = result_1ch["queue_fifo"].to(microsecond)
    own_read_1ch = result_1ch["own_read"].to(microsecond)
    backlogs_sense_1ch = math.floor(((sense - own_read_1ch) / queue_1ch).to("dimensionless").magnitude)
    backlogs_wcet_1ch = math.floor(((wcet_read_ceiling - own_read_1ch) / queue_1ch).to("dimensionless").magnitude)

    # ┌── 3. GUARD ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    check(result["queued_transactions"] == 88 and result["tile_transactions"] == 64, "88 queued transactions, 64 of them from one tile.")
    check(abs(bandwidth.to("GB/s").magnitude - 204.0) < 1e-9, "The application SoC's registry bandwidth is 204 GB/s.")
    check(abs(queue.magnitude - 1.8794) < 5e-4, "360,448 bytes at 204 GB/s plus three 37.5 ns conflicts is 1.879 µs.")
    check(loaded_read < sense, "One backlog fits inside the sense allowance.")
    check(abs(read_ceiling.magnitude - 305.0) < 1e-9, "The deadline leaves 305 µs for the read after 95 µs of compute.")
    check(backlogs_sense == 21 and backlogs_deadline == 162, "The sense allowance absorbs 21 backlogs, the deadline 162.")
    check(abs(wcet_read_ceiling.magnitude - 155.0) < 1e-9 and backlogs_wcet == 82, "The declared WCET leaves 155 µs for the read, 82 backlogs.")
    check(bypass_read < own_read * 3, "Priority bypass leaves one in-flight transaction ahead of the read.")
    check(n_channels == 16, "A 256-bit interface of 16-bit LPDDR5 channels has 16 channels.")
    check(backlogs_sense_1ch == 1 and backlogs_wcet_1ch == 5, "Confined to one channel, the sense allowance absorbs 1 backlog and the WCET 5.")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    sense_str = fmt_latency(sense, unit=microsecond, precision=0)
    compute_after_sense_str = fmt_latency(compute_after_sense, unit=microsecond, precision=0)
    deadline_str = fmt_latency(deadline, unit=microsecond, precision=0)
    n_tx_str = fmt_int(result["queued_transactions"])
    tile_tx_str = fmt_int(result["tile_transactions"])
    backlog_bytes_str = fmt_int(backlog_bytes)
    snapshot_bytes_str = fmt_int(snapshot_bytes)
    queue_str = fmt(queue.magnitude, precision=3)
    own_read_str = fmt(own_read.magnitude, precision=3)
    loaded_read_str = fmt(loaded_read.magnitude, precision=3)
    sense_left_str = fmt(sense_left.magnitude, precision=2)
    read_ceiling_str = fmt_latency(read_ceiling, unit=microsecond, precision=0)
    backlogs_deadline_str = fmt_int(backlogs_deadline)
    wcet_str = fmt_latency(wcet, unit=microsecond, precision=0)
    wcet_read_ceiling_str = fmt_latency(wcet_read_ceiling, unit=microsecond, precision=0)
    backlogs_wcet_str = fmt_int(backlogs_wcet)
    bypass_read_str = fmt(bypass_read.magnitude, precision=2)
    bandwidth_str = fmt(bandwidth.to("GB/s").magnitude, precision=0)
    backlogs_sense_str = fmt_int(backlogs_sense)
    bank_switch_str = fmt(bank_switch_time.to("ns").magnitude, precision=1)
    bank_switches_str = fmt_int(bank_switches)
    n_channels_str = fmt_int(n_channels)
    queue_1ch_str = fmt(queue_1ch.magnitude, precision=1)
    backlogs_sense_1ch_str = fmt_int(backlogs_sense_1ch)
    backlogs_wcet_1ch_str = fmt_int(backlogs_wcet_1ch)
```

::: {#nbk-placement-loaded-read .callout-notebook title="Loaded read latency on a shared die"}

**Problem**: Suppose the permission path read its sensor snapshot from the application SoC's shared DRAM. How much queued traffic could precede that read before the tick exceeds its sense allowance, its declared worst-case execution time, and its deadline?

**Variables**: The tick allots `{python} PlacementLoadedRead.sense_str` to sensing and `{python} PlacementLoadedRead.compute_after_sense_str` to constraint evaluation and the drive-frame write, inside a `{python} PlacementLoadedRead.deadline_str` deadline. The snapshot is `{python} PlacementLoadedRead.snapshot_bytes_str` bytes in the application SoC's DRAM, whose peak bandwidth is `{python} PlacementLoadedRead.bandwidth_str` GB/s. The controller interleaves physical addresses across all of its channels, so the snapshot and the traffic ahead of it are served at that aggregate rate. Ahead of it the FIFO holds one weight tile (`{python} PlacementLoadedRead.tile_tx_str` transactions), a camera transfer, and a telemetry record: `{python} PlacementLoadedRead.n_tx_str` transactions, `{python} PlacementLoadedRead.backlog_bytes_str` bytes, `{python} PlacementLoadedRead.bank_switches_str` same-bank row conflicts.

**Math**: By @eq-placement-dram-queuing, serving the backlog's `{python} PlacementLoadedRead.backlog_bytes_str` bytes at `{python} PlacementLoadedRead.bandwidth_str` GB/s, plus `{python} PlacementLoadedRead.bank_switches_str` row-conflict penalties of `{python} PlacementLoadedRead.bank_switch_str` ns, takes `{python} PlacementLoadedRead.queue_str` $\mu\text{s}$. The snapshot itself reads in `{python} PlacementLoadedRead.own_read_str` $\mu\text{s}$, so the loaded read takes `{python} PlacementLoadedRead.loaded_read_str` $\mu\text{s}$ and leaves `{python} PlacementLoadedRead.sense_left_str` $\mu\text{s}$ of the sense allowance, which absorbs `{python} PlacementLoadedRead.backlogs_sense_str` such backlogs before it overruns. The declared worst-case execution time of `{python} PlacementLoadedRead.wcet_str` is crossed once the read exceeds `{python} PlacementLoadedRead.wcet_read_ceiling_str`, which takes more than `{python} PlacementLoadedRead.backlogs_wcet_str` backlogs, and that crossing refutes the declared execution bound even though the tick still meets its deadline. It does not by itself refute the weaker claim that this load preserves the deadline. The deadline itself holds until the read exceeds `{python} PlacementLoadedRead.read_ceiling_str`, which takes more than `{python} PlacementLoadedRead.backlogs_deadline_str` backlogs, so meeting the deadline does not establish the stronger declared execution bound. With validated priority bypass, only the one in-flight transaction waits ahead, and the read takes `{python} PlacementLoadedRead.bypass_read_str` $\mu\text{s}$.

**Systems insight**: The read's bound belongs to the memory controller, not to the workload. The bound exists only if the controller limits how much traffic it admits ahead of a safety read or lets that read bypass the queue, and an FR-FCFS controller serving a streaming accelerator provides neither unless its configuration is qualified to do so. At the SoC's full bandwidth, though, plain queueing is a weak threat: the allowance absorbs `{python} PlacementLoadedRead.backlogs_sense_str` backlogs. The interleaving premise carries much of that result. If the backlog and the snapshot shared one of the interface's `{python} PlacementLoadedRead.n_channels_str` channels, each backlog would take `{python} PlacementLoadedRead.queue_1ch_str` $\mu\text{s}$, the allowance would absorb `{python} PlacementLoadedRead.backlogs_sense_1ch_str`, and more than `{python} PlacementLoadedRead.backlogs_wcet_1ch_str` would cross the declared bound, so the address mapping belongs in the placement evidence. The mechanisms that actually threaten the declared bound are the ones this FIFO model omits, which @sec-placement-interference-mechanisms prices next.

:::

@Fig-13-loaded-tick draws the notebook's thresholds on the tick's own time axis. Each row is one tick with a given number of backlogs queued ahead of the snapshot read, so the reader can see how much traffic separates the sense allowance, the declared bound, and the deadline, and how much less it takes when the backlog shares the snapshot's channel.

::: {#fig-13-loaded-tick fig-env="figure" fig-pos="t" fig-cap="**How many backlogs one tick absorbs**: Each row is one permission tick on the rejected shared-die placement, drawn to scale on the 1 ms period, with the FIFO wait for queued backlogs ahead of the snapshot read followed by the `{python} PlacementLoadedRead.compute_after_sense_str` of constraint evaluation and drive-frame write. With addresses interleaved across the interface, `{python} PlacementLoadedRead.backlogs_sense_str` backlogs fit the sense allowance, `{python} PlacementLoadedRead.backlogs_wcet_str` the declared bound, and `{python} PlacementLoadedRead.backlogs_deadline_str` the deadline; confined to one channel, `{python} PlacementLoadedRead.backlogs_wcet_1ch_str` already reach the declared bound. Every row still ends well inside the period, which is why the declared bound, not the period, is the test the placement must pass." fig-alt="Horizontal bar chart on a time axis from 0 to 1,000 microseconds with five rows. The top row is the unloaded tick: a 40 microsecond sense read and 95 microseconds of constraint evaluation and write, ending at 135. Below it, rows with 21, 82, and 162 queued backlogs show a hatched memory wait growing until the tick ends near 135, 250, and 400 microseconds. The bottom row, with 5 backlogs confined to one memory channel, ends near 237 microseconds. Vertical lines mark the end of the sense allowance at 40, the declared worst-case execution time at 250, the deadline at 400, and the next tick at 1,000 microseconds."}

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ THE LOADED PERMISSION TICK, TO SCALE (FIGURE)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @fig-13-loaded-tick
# │
# │ Goal: Show the notebook's backlog thresholds on one tick's time axis.
# │ Show: the unloaded tick, then the tick at the largest backlog count that
# │       keeps each bound (sense allowance, declared WCET, deadline), and
# │       the one-channel case at the WCET, against the 1 ms period.
# │ How: PlacementMachine sub-costs and PlacementLoadedRead's FIFO model
# │      (calc_axi_fifo_contention); no new inputs.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import viz
from mlsysim.core.units import microsecond
from mlsysim.fmt import check

PM = PlacementMachine
LR = PlacementLoadedRead
viz.set_book_style()
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from matplotlib.patches import Patch

C = viz.COLORS

# ┌── 1. LOAD ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
def us(q):
    return q.to(microsecond).magnitude

sense, compute = us(PM.sense), us(LR.compute_after_sense)
wcet, deadline, tick = us(PM.wcet), us(PM.deadline), us(PM.tick)
q, own = us(LR.queue), us(LR.own_read)
q1, own1 = us(LR.queue_1ch), us(LR.own_read_1ch)

# ┌── 2. EXECUTE ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# (label, queued wait, snapshot read, compute after sense)
rows = [
    ("unloaded", 0.0, sense, compute),
    (f"{LR.backlogs_sense} backlogs", LR.backlogs_sense * q, own, compute),
    (f"{LR.backlogs_wcet} backlogs", LR.backlogs_wcet * q, own, compute),
    (f"{LR.backlogs_deadline} backlogs", LR.backlogs_deadline * q, own, compute),
    (f"{LR.backlogs_wcet_1ch} backlogs,\none channel", LR.backlogs_wcet_1ch * q1, own1, compute),
]
ends = [w + r + c for _, w, r, c in rows]

# ┌── 3. GUARD ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
check(abs(ends[0] - us(PM.unloaded)) < 1e-9, "The unloaded row is the 135 µs tick.")
check(rows[1][1] + rows[1][2] <= sense, "The sense row's read fits the sense allowance.")
check(ends[2] <= wcet < ends[2] + q, "The WCET row is the largest backlog count within the declared bound.")
check(ends[3] <= deadline < ends[3] + q, "The deadline row is the largest backlog count within the deadline.")
check(ends[4] <= wcet < ends[4] + q1, "The one-channel row is the largest count within the declared bound.")
check(max(ends) < tick, "Every row ends inside the 1 ms period.")

# ┌── 4. PLOT ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 3.9))
ys = list(range(len(rows)))[::-1]
for y, (lab, w, r, c), end in zip(ys, rows, ends):
    if w > 0:
        ax.barh(y, w, left=0, height=0.56, color=C["BlueL"], edgecolor=C["BlueLine"], hatch="////", lw=0.8, zorder=3)
    ax.barh(y, r, left=w, height=0.56, color=C["BlueLine"], edgecolor=C["BlueLine"], lw=0.8, zorder=3)
    ax.barh(y, c, left=w + r, height=0.56, color=C["OrangeL"], edgecolor=C["OrangeLine"], lw=0.8, zorder=3)
    x_lab = end + 10
    for x_line in (wcet, deadline):
        if end <= x_line < end + 60:
            x_lab = x_line + 8
    ax.text(x_lab, y, f"{end:.0f} µs", ha="left", va="center", fontsize=9, color=C["primary"], zorder=4)
for x, lab, col, ls in [
    (sense, "sense\nallowance", C["BlueLine"], (0, (2, 2))),
    (wcet, "declared\nWCET", C["primary"], (0, (5, 3))),
    (deadline, "deadline", C["RedLine"], "-"),
    (tick, "next tick", C["grid"], (0, (4, 3))),
]:
    ax.axvline(x, color=col, lw=1.2, ls=ls, zorder=2)
    ha, dx = ("right", -6) if x >= tick else ("left", 6)
    ax.text(x + dx, len(rows) - 0.35, lab, ha=ha, va="bottom", fontsize=8.5, color=col if col != C["grid"] else C["primary"])
ax.set_yticks(ys)
ax.set_yticklabels([r[0] for r in rows], fontsize=9)
ax.set_xlim(0, tick + 20)
ax.set_ylim(-0.6, len(rows) + 0.25)
ax.set_xticks([0, 100, 200, 300, 400, 500, 600, 700, 800, 900, 1000])
ax.set_xlabel("Time within one 1 ms tick (µs)")
ax.grid(axis="y", visible=False)
ax.legend(
    handles=[
        Patch(facecolor=C["BlueL"], edgecolor=C["BlueLine"], hatch="////", label="wait for queued backlogs"),
        Patch(facecolor=C["BlueLine"], edgecolor=C["BlueLine"], label="snapshot read (sense)"),
        Patch(facecolor=C["OrangeL"], edgecolor=C["OrangeLine"], label="constraints + drive-frame write"),
    ],
    loc="lower right",
    bbox_to_anchor=(0.93, 0.0),
    fontsize=8.5,
    frameon=False,

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

### Which interference mechanism threatens the declared bound {#sec-placement-interference-mechanisms}

```{python}
#| label: calc-placement-interference-mechanisms
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ WHICH MECHANISM THREATENS THE DECLARED WCET
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-placement-interference-mechanisms, @sec-placement-summary
# │
# │ Goal: Compare the stretch the permission tick can absorb with measured
# │       shared-cache interference on embedded multicores, and find the
# │       memory-stall share of the tick at which each measured slowdown
# │       crosses the declared WCET.
# │ Show: WCET / unloaded = 1.85x, deadline / unloaded = 2.96x; measured MSHR
# │       contention 21x (Valsan et al. 2016, with cache partitioning) and
# │       writeback-buffer DoS >300x (Bechtel and Yun 2019). If a stall share
# │       f of the 135 µs tick is slowed by S, the WCET holds only for
# │       f <= (1.85 - 1) / (S - 1): 4.3 percent at 21x, 0.28 percent at 300x.
# │ How: registry WCET, deadline, and unloaded tick; slowdowns are published
# │      measurements on other platforms (not the Orin), used as multipliers;
# │      calc_stall_share_breakeven (Amdahl's fixed-fraction model read as a
# │      slowdown) for the break-even shares.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.physics import calc_partial_slowdown_stretch, calc_stall_share_breakeven
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt, fmt_percent, fmt_multiple, check

class PlacementInterference:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    unloaded = PlacementMachine.unloaded  # category: illustrative (registry)
    wcet = PlacementMachine.wcet  # category: chosen (declared)
    deadline = PlacementMachine.deadline  # category: chosen
    s_mshr = 21.0  # category: measured (Valsan, Yun, Farshchi, RTAS 2016: up to 21x WCET increase, MSHR contention, cache partitioned)
    s_wb = 300.0  # category: measured (Bechtel and Yun, RTAS 2019: >300x on a dedicated core; lower bound of the reported range)

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    stretch_wcet = (wcet / unloaded).to("dimensionless").magnitude
    stretch_deadline = (deadline / unloaded).to("dimensionless").magnitude
    f_mshr = calc_stall_share_breakeven(stretch_wcet, s_mshr)
    f_wb = calc_stall_share_breakeven(stretch_wcet, s_wb)
    f_mshr_deadline = calc_stall_share_breakeven(stretch_deadline, s_mshr)

    # ┌── 3. GUARD ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    check(abs(stretch_wcet - 250 / 135) < 1e-9 and abs(stretch_deadline - 400 / 135) < 1e-9, "250/135 and 400/135.")
    check(s_mshr > stretch_deadline and s_wb > 100 * stretch_wcet, "Measured slowdowns exceed the tick's absorbable stretch.")
    check(abs(f_mshr - 0.0426) < 5e-4 and abs(f_wb - 0.00285) < 5e-5, "Break-even stall shares: 4.3 and 0.28 percent.")
    check(abs(calc_partial_slowdown_stretch(f_mshr, s_mshr) - stretch_wcet) < 1e-9, "At the break-even share the tick lands exactly on the WCET.")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    stretch_wcet_str = fmt(stretch_wcet, precision=2)
    stretch_deadline_str = fmt(stretch_deadline, precision=2)
    s_mshr_mult_str = fmt_multiple(s_mshr, precision=0)
    s_wb_mult_str = fmt_multiple(s_wb, precision=0)
    f_mshr_pct_str = fmt_percent(f_mshr, precision=1)
    f_wb_pct_str = fmt_percent(f_wb, precision=2)
    f_mshr_deadline_pct_str = fmt_percent(f_mshr_deadline, precision=1)
```

The notebook's arithmetic makes the shared die look safe, and that impression is the danger. The permission tick can absorb a stretch of its unloaded `{python} PlacementMachine.unloaded_str` cycle by a factor of `{python} PlacementInterference.stretch_wcet_str` before it crosses the declared worst-case execution time, and by `{python} PlacementInterference.stretch_deadline_str` before it crosses the deadline. Bandwidth queueing at the SoC's full rate does not come close. Two other mechanisms do, and both live in the shared cache rather than in DRAM.

A non-blocking cache tracks each outstanding miss in a *miss status holding register* (MSHR) and parks each dirty line it evicts in a *writeback buffer* until DRAM accepts it. Both structures are small and shared by every core behind the cache. When a streaming co-runner keeps them full, each miss of the victim core waits until an entry drains, so the victim's delay grows with its own miss count times the aggressor's drain time, not with the bytes it reads. Partitioning cache capacity does not help, because the partition divides the lines and leaves the MSHRs and the writeback buffer shared. Measured on commercial embedded multicores, MSHR contention raised a task's worst-case execution time by up to `{python} PlacementInterference.s_mshr_mult_str` with the cache partitioned [@valsan2016taming], and a deliberate attack on the writeback buffer slowed a victim on a dedicated core by more than `{python} PlacementInterference.s_wb_mult_str`, partitioned or not [@bechtel2019denial]. DRAM adds its own multiplier on top. An analytical bound for commercial controllers shows that each of the victim's requests can wait behind every request that other cores may place ahead of it in the same bank, a number set by queue depth and the reordering window rather than by average bandwidth [@kim2014bounding].

These slowdowns were measured on other platforms, on victims whose time was mostly memory stall, so they cannot be charged to the enforcer directly. They can be charged to its memory-stall share. If a fraction $f$ of the unloaded tick waits on shared-cache misses and interference slows that fraction by a factor $S$ while the rest runs unchanged, the tick takes $t_{\text{unloaded}}[(1-f) + fS] = t_{\text{unloaded}}[1 + f(S-1)]$. Setting that no larger than $C_{\text{wcet}}$ and solving for $f$ shows that the declared bound survives only while
$$f \le \frac{C_{\text{wcet}}/t_{\text{unloaded}} - 1}{S - 1}.$$
At the MSHR-class `{python} PlacementInterference.s_mshr_mult_str`, the declared bound falls once more than `{python} PlacementInterference.f_mshr_pct_str` percent of the tick is miss stall, and the deadline once more than `{python} PlacementInterference.f_mshr_deadline_pct_str` percent is. At the writeback-buffer attack's `{python} PlacementInterference.s_wb_mult_str`, the threshold is `{python} PlacementInterference.f_wb_pct_str` percent. A constraint evaluation that touches tables in shared memory easily exceeds those fractions. The mechanism that threatens the declared bound is therefore miss handling in the shared cache, amplified by bank queueing, and the only placements that remove it are those whose tick runs from private memory: candidates (c) and (d) of @tbl-13-placement-candidates. On (a) and (b), the measured stall share on the target and a regulation mechanism that bounds $S$ (@sec-placement-isolation-decisions) are what a qualification must supply.

### Power-rail interference

A sudden motor or accelerator current demand can lower the voltage available to a controller sharing its supply. The first-order package model is
$$\Delta V_{\text{droop}} = L_{\text{pkg}} \frac{dI}{dt} + \Delta I \cdot R_{\text{pkg}}$$
The placement decision depends on whether regulation, decoupling, and stored energy keep the permission path inside its characterized operating range. The package hierarchy and transistor-level derivation are developed in @sec-appendix-systems-droop; here the model identifies the disturbance that the chosen rail must survive.

```{python}
#| label: calc-placement-inductive-pdn-droop
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
from mlsysim.core.units import ureg, nanosecond
from mlsysim.physics.robotics import (
    calc_voltage_droop,
    calc_inductive_voltage_droop,
    calc_alpha_power_gate_delay_stretch,
)
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt, fmt_int, fmt_percent

class InductivePDNVoltageDroop:
    v_core = 0.850 * ureg.volt  # category: illustrative
    l_pkg = 30.0 * ureg.picohenry  # category: illustrative
    r_pkg = 8.0 * ureg.milliohm  # category: illustrative
    delta_i = 6.0 * ureg.ampere  # category: illustrative
    t_rise = 2.0 * nanosecond  # category: illustrative
    di_dt = delta_i / t_rise

    v_ind = calc_inductive_voltage_droop(l_pkg, di_dt)
    v_res = calc_voltage_droop(delta_i, r_pkg)
    v_droop = v_ind + v_res
    v_drooped = v_core - v_droop

    v_th = 0.420 * ureg.volt  # category: illustrative
    alpha = 1.3  # category: illustrative
    res_stretch = calc_alpha_power_gate_delay_stretch(
        nominal_voltage=v_core,
        drooped_voltage=v_drooped,
        threshold_voltage=v_th,
        alpha=alpha,
    )
    delay_expansion_pct = res_stretch["delay_expansion_percent"]

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Format & Export) ────────────────────────────────────────
    v_th_str = fmt(v_th.to(ureg.volt).magnitude, precision=3)
    alpha_str = fmt(alpha, precision=1)
    v_core_str = fmt(v_core.to(ureg.volt).magnitude, precision=2)
    v_core_3dec_str = fmt(v_core.to(ureg.volt).magnitude, precision=3)
    l_pkg_str = fmt(l_pkg.to(ureg.picohenry).magnitude, precision=0)
    r_pkg_str = fmt(r_pkg.to(ureg.milliohm).magnitude, precision=0)
    delta_i_str = fmt(delta_i.to(ureg.ampere).magnitude, precision=0)
    t_rise_str = fmt(t_rise.to(nanosecond).magnitude, precision=0)
    v_ind_mv_str = fmt(v_ind.to(ureg.millivolt).magnitude, precision=0)
    v_res_mv_str = fmt(v_res.to(ureg.millivolt).magnitude, precision=0)
    v_droop_mv_str = fmt(v_droop.to(ureg.millivolt).magnitude, precision=0)
    v_droop_v_str = fmt(v_droop.to(ureg.volt).magnitude, precision=3)
    v_drooped_str = fmt(v_drooped.to(ureg.volt).magnitude, precision=3)
    droop_pct_str = fmt_percent((v_droop / v_core).magnitude, precision=1)
    delay_expansion_pct_str = fmt_int(round(delay_expansion_pct))
```

For the illustrative package parameters, a `{python} InductivePDNVoltageDroop.delta_i_str` A step with a `{python} InductivePDNVoltageDroop.t_rise_str` ns rise through `{python} InductivePDNVoltageDroop.l_pkg_str` pH gives `{python} InductivePDNVoltageDroop.v_ind_mv_str` mV of inductive droop, and the same step through `{python} InductivePDNVoltageDroop.r_pkg_str` m$\Omega$ gives `{python} InductivePDNVoltageDroop.v_res_mv_str` mV of resistive droop, `{python} InductivePDNVoltageDroop.v_droop_mv_str` mV in all from a `{python} InductivePDNVoltageDroop.v_core_3dec_str` V nominal rail. This pure $L\,dI/dt$ term ignores on-die decoupling capacitance, so it overstates the first droop; power-integrity engineers instead design the delivery network to a target impedance across frequency, and the first droop is set by package inductance resonating with on-die capacitance. The alpha-power model [@sakurai1990alpha] relates the resulting voltage to gate delay:
$$\frac{t_{\text{prop}}(V_{\text{drooped}})}{t_{\text{prop}}(V_{\text{nominal}})} = \frac{V_{\text{drooped}}}{V_{\text{nominal}}} \left( \frac{V_{\text{nominal}} - V_{\text{th}}}{V_{\text{drooped}} - V_{\text{th}}} \right)^\alpha$$
Here $V_{\text{th}}$ is the modeled threshold voltage, stipulated as `{python} InductivePDNVoltageDroop.v_th_str` V, and $\alpha$ is the technology-dependent exponent, stipulated as `{python} InductivePDNVoltageDroop.alpha_str`. With those inputs, the modeled delay increases by `{python} InductivePDNVoltageDroop.delay_expansion_pct_str` percent. This is a sensitivity calculation, not a measured reset threshold or a universal delay increase for every gate, and it is an upper-bound caricature because it ignores decoupling. The stretch lasts nanoseconds, so it does not lengthen the tick by that percentage; it threatens the setup-time margin of the paths switching during the droop, and it grows without bound as the drooped voltage approaches $V_{\text{th}}$. Many current processors detect the droop and stretch the clock until the rail recovers [@grenat2014adaptive], which turns a timing violation into lost cycles that the tick must absorb. Device characterization must establish whether the actual critical paths still meet setup time, how many cycles adaptive clocking removes, and whether undervoltage protection trips.

A separate permission rail removes the modeled shared core-supply path, but the common battery, wiring, converter behavior, and return paths remain qualification obligations. Rail probes and independent timing instruments must observe them under simultaneous motor and proposal load. Droop and queueing both end within microseconds of the burst that causes them. The heat that the same accelerator dissipates does not, and it couples the paths on a timescale a million times longer.

## Thermal and Timing Coupling {#sec-placement-thermal-timing-coupling}

The permission core can slow down after the proposal workload has stopped, because stored heat takes time to leave the package. Thermal coupling therefore requires a longer test than the short current step or memory burst. When the accelerator and permission core share a thermal path and governor, sustained proposal power can change the clock available to enforcement.
